From prehistory to the ancient Romans

In the homogeneous stretch of the Apennines lying between the river Scrivia to the West, the river Taro to the East, the Po to the North and the Ligurian Sea to the South, the first settlements date back to the Lower Palaeolithic, in the final phase of the cultural horizon known as the “Acheulean”, 150,000 years ago. Moreover, all the pass areas of the region have been frequented at least since the Mesolithic, as documented in all the Ligurian archaeological museums.

In the days of the pre-Roman peoples, the Celtic and Ligurian civilisations were intertwined from the Iron Age onwards. Little has survived in writing of their presence, but many legends remain, handed down over time by the local populations, as well as some place names. M. Penna itself, which separates the Aveto valley from the Ceno valley, would seem to derive from the god “Pen” and is said to give its name to the whole Italian Apennine range. Other places in Val Trebbia and Val d’Aveto, such as Amborzasco (from the Celtic “ambros”, strong man), seem to bear the marks of the presence of Celtic peoples.

It was, however, in the time of the Romans that these places began to be the stage of encounters and clashes with the Ligurians, from the 3rd century B.C. onwards. The Latin historians – Livy, Strabo and Polybius – relate that the Romans took no fewer than 80 years to subdue the warlike Ligurian Veleiates, who had occupied the Genoese mountains since time immemorial. They had to flush them out of hilltops, ridges, gorges and ravines in the most remote valleys, falling into constant traps and snares and losing a considerable number of men and resources. It is, however, also plausible that the innermost areas seemed inhospitable to the Romans, as indeed they have been during many other long periods. This would seem to be borne out by the milder treatment reserved for the Ligurian Veleiates compared with the Ligurian Apuani of Lunigiana, a region the Romans considered far more strategic. One may then imagine that, even in those days, the steep slopes of the Trebbia and the Aveto lent themselves much more to adventure and travel than to comfort and settled life.

The clash with the Ligurians was not the only major confrontation the Romans had in the area. In 218 B.C., the same year as the Roman foundation of Piacenza, the famous “battle of the Trebbia” between Romans and Carthaginians took place near Ancarano (a hamlet of Rivergaro), already on the plain. About this battle, about Hannibal’s descent with his elephants across the Alps and the Apennines, about his passage through Val Boreca, about the place names of probable Carthaginian origin (Pej, Cartasegna, Tartago, Bogli, Zerba, Suzzi) and about the way the Carthaginians routed the Romans, a great deal has already been said and written, and it is not worth lingering over. Some less familiar aspects concern the actual route Hannibal followed to reach the upper part of Val Boreca, whose torrent of the same name is a left-bank tributary of the Trebbia. Among the various hypotheses put forward by historians, one also involves a crossing of what a few centuries later would become the Strada del Cifalco. It is in fact surmised that he reached Val Boreca by cutting perpendicularly across the Trebbia-Aveto ridge at Passo Ertola: the name of this Pass, too, would appear to be of Carthaginian stamp.

The Early Middle Ages: Lombards, monasteries and the first paths in the Ligurian Apennines

Not even the discovery – at Veleia, in 1747 – of the “Tabula Alimentaria Traianea”, perhaps the most important find of the whole Latin civilisation, dating from the 2nd century A.D., allows any firm speculation about what happened (and what was still to happen in the future) at the time when the barbarian invasions spread. In fact, in the Apennines between the Taro and the Scrivia, the first mark after the Romans was left by the Lombards. Between 636 and 652 A.D., several kings issued grants for the foundation of monasteries, following hot on the heels of that of San Colombano at Bobbio, in Val Trebbia, the first to be founded in the region, in 614.

The monks began to build not only monasteries, but also cenobia and cells, conceived for praying and tilling the fields, and hospices where xenodochia, that is the hospitality of travellers, was practised. They then created paths and tracks to link these buildings to one another, until they shaped a genuine ancient road network. With the spread of pilgrimages to Rome and to the holy places of the East, the religious use of these routes, known as “viae pubblicae pellegrinorum” (“public roads of the pilgrims”), grew considerably.

It is not possible to state whether some stretches of the Antica Via del Cifalco were originally opened by the monks, just as it cannot be asserted of any other path in the area; but one can with certainty attribute to the monks an indirect effect that served to increase the popularity of the Strada del Cifalco within the wider road network of the upper Val d’Aveto. Indeed, according to the accounts handed down, the draining and reclamation of the enormous lake of Cabanne (where today there remains a plain furrowed by the Aveto) were the work of Benedictine monks in the 12th century. By clearing the riverbed, they eliminated the basin, encouraging the routes of communication and the local trade as they then developed right up to modern times.

It is in any case beyond doubt that this wide network of paths was later taken up for commercial, military and civil purposes too, and that part of it can still be used today. It therefore represents the first tangible sign that History has left as a characteristic element of the landscape of this part of the Apennines.

The Late Middle Ages: Malaspina, Fieschi, Doria

The first real political upheavals in the region took place in the feudal world, from the 8th century onwards; or, at least, this is where the History of the Antica Via del Cifalco really comes alive.

At that time, the lands between the Taro and the Scrivia were fragmented into small fiefs run by great families. In the territories between the Trebbia and the Aveto, a dominant role was played by the Malaspina dynasty. This family in fact embodies the second version of feudalism, rather than the initial one of the “curtis” (or court), founded on a self-sufficient agricultural and economic unit. The second phase, that of the “seigneuries” which developed from the 11th century, was characterised by the exercise of the function of governing complex political and legal relationships.

It was Frederick I Hohenstaufen, better known as Frederick Barbarossa (1122-1190, in power as Emperor of the Romans from 1152 until his death), who invested the Malaspina with the feudal diploma in 1164, as part of his design that saw these structures as an indispensable condition for holding the Empire together.

He was the protagonist of a famous episode in which he walked the Antica Via del Cifalco in person, in 1167. That year, the Emperor was in Rome, where he had managed to install the antipope Paschal III, an operation brought to a successful conclusion and crowned by his second coronation. He thus seemed on the verge of triumph, with the true pope Alexander III a refugee in Benevento; that is, until a devastating plague epidemic struck the Eternal City, which was immediately interpreted as a dark divine punishment and an omen of misfortune. He therefore decided to return to the North, but found the Monte Bardone road closed by the people of Pontremoli and by the Lombard League.

It was Obizzo Malaspina, himself a protégé of the Emperor, who got him out of trouble by escorting him as far as Tortona by an alternative route through the midst of his fiefs. They crossed Lunigiana and reached the Cifalco “by narrow and winding ways, at great peril to our person and to so great an army”, as the Emperor himself declared. During the journey, it seems that Frederick Barbarossa, curious about the way of life in those inhospitable places, asked the Marquis Malaspina what he lived on. “De toltis”, that is “on things taken”, the latter candidly replied, leaving historians, moreover, with some doubt as to what he was really alluding to: was he referring to hunting and fishing? Or to the robberies of the brigands under his protection? Or yet again to every sum his vassals collected on the commercial traffic along the ridge? According to a second hypothesis, the exact phrase was instead “de vultis” (or “de voltis”), referring to what the valley folk long called “le volte”, that is the places where goods and caravans halted, or else to the architectural features where trade was carried out in the villages. The doubt will probably never be dispelled, but to us – considering the historical context as a whole and the enormous number of people who lived in a grey area just on this side or the other of legality, often with the lord’s placet – the first hypothesis seems the more plausible.

Over time, however, the small fiefs between the Trebbia and the Aveto struggled to withstand the advance of the Free Communes (from the 11th century and then more markedly from the 12th century, up to the 13th century), especially those of Piacenza and Parma, eager to open trade routes between the plain and the sea. The rise of these Communes led to the gradual shift of the Apennine trade routes towards the valley floors. For them, this was the only way to break the control the Malaspina exercised over the mountains with their strongholds, above all those of Cariseto and Oneto.

After 500 years of dominion over the ridge between the Trebbia and the Aveto (and beyond), the Malaspina began to decline rapidly from the beginning of the 17th century. This was the result of the continual subdivision of the fiefs among the descendants, but also of the growing difficulty in collecting levies in a world that would no longer tolerate them. Speaking of which: according to tradition, the name of the house derives precisely from their methods of government, which were certainly not democratic. But there is a more evocative legend, told on the entrance portal of the Palazzo Malaspina at Godiasco: in 540, the supposed founder of the dynasty – Azzino Marzio – is said to have avenged the death of his father, caused by the king of the Franks Theudebert at the time of the siege of the city of Milan, by piercing him with a thorn. Hence the desperate cry of the dying man, “Ah, mala spina!”; but also the centuries-old family motto: “Sum mala spina bonis, sum bona spina malis”.

Descended, like the Malaspina, from the original Obertenghi stock, the Fieschi were already influential when Innocent IV, a member of the family, was elected Pope in 1243. Enterprising and pro-French, they reached the height of their power in the 15th century, as shown by the alliance agreement concluded with the Malaspina in 1495. Many of the fiefs adjoining the Antica Via del Cifalco, most of which had formerly belonged to the Malaspina, passed into the hands of the Fieschi during their heyday.

Here a digression is needed, since it was precisely in the period of the Fieschi’s greatest splendour that one of the most iconic episodes of local history took place. This was the failed “Fieschi conspiracy” of 1547.

Gian Luigi Fieschi, an ambitious and charismatic young man, decided to lay a trap for the Doria, who had acquired such economic and political power in the Genoa area as to progressively marginalise the influence his family had exercised of old.

He gathered a group of his most loyal followers, including Genoese nobles, and other mercenaries. He organised the action for the night between 2 and 3 January 1547. The plan was to take control of the city with two key moves: seizing the Doria ships moored in the harbour and assassinating Giannettino Doria, nephew and heir of Andrea Doria, but also disliked by the population and therefore a “political” target as well, so that the conspiracy would win over the hearts of the people.

The plan, however, failed disastrously. As he was preparing to board one of the Doria ships, Gian Luigi Fieschi slipped into the sea in all his heavy armour and drowned. The conspirators were thrown into confusion and the group soon fell apart, in panic.

At dawn, Andrea Doria reacted with ferocity. The conspirators fled the city. One of the most significant groups, led by Gerolamo Fieschi, took refuge in the castle of Cariseto. It was on this occasion that they travelled the entire Via del Cifalco, pursued by Andrea Doria’s men. It was in fact the shortest road to one of the most impregnable fortresses of their possessions. The castle of Cariseto was one of the last rebel strongholds to hold out but, since it was impossible to withstand the siege, Gerolamo Fieschi, with 120 Apennine subjects and 30 mercenary soldiers, fled in the night through a tunnel that led into the woods, in a frantic race to the last place where they could take refuge: the castle of Montoggio, above Torriglia, in Valle Scrivia on the borders of the upper Valtrebbia. There too, they long resisted the Doria attacks, but in vain: it was the mercenaries themselves who betrayed them, seizing the keep and letting the enemy into the castle. After a summary trial, Gerolamo Fieschi was beheaded. The castle of Montoggio was destroyed, although the thickness of its walls forced the sappers to work another two years to complete the job.

The catastrophic outcome of the conspiracy and the reprisals that followed brought an abrupt end to the influence this house had exercised between the Trebbia and the Aveto, as in other areas of the Apennines. It lost all its fiefs to the Doria, with the placet of the Emperor Charles V, and was wiped off the political scene.

The famous Fieschi conspiracy has inspired a great number of artists, who have offered various reworkings of it, such as Friedrich Schiller’s play of 1783 and the 1921 silent film directed by Ugo Falena.

And so the Doria too came to play a prominent role in these territories: among other things, they had a fortified palace built at Gorreto and purchased the Castle of Ottone, lying below the Strada del Cifalco.

They dominated the northern Apennine scene for a long time. Once the Fieschi had been swept away, a fierce rivalry flared up with the Farnese, who ruled the Duchy of Parma and Piacenza from 1545 to 1731. The dispute culminated in the Doria’s occupation of the castle of Borgo Taro in 1636, which was followed – in retaliation – by the Farnese seizure of the Castle of Santo Stefano d’Aveto in the same year. A peace treaty of 1637 returned to each of the two families what had been wrongfully taken and allowed the Doria to consolidate their hegemony over the Apennine lands until the Modern Era.

Napoleon and the end of the Ligurian Imperial Fiefs

In 1796, Napoleon had established his headquarters at Tortona, in today’s province of Alessandria. This move provoked an immediate revolt by the population, who had no intention of giving up their self-determination in choosing their forms of government. Driven by the aim of stemming these protests over the administration of the territory, Napoleon in person put an end to the long history of the Ligurian Imperial Fiefs, which had begun with Frederick Barbarossa, with the ordinance of Arquata Scrivia, later ratified by the Treaty of Campoformio in 1797.

From then on, many young men of Val Trebbia were conscripted obtorto collo for the Napoleonic campaigns; but the French gendarmes, charged with pursuing the many deserters into the mountains, more often than not came back empty-handed.

After Napoleon’s defeats, the Congress of Vienna of 1815 decreed the annexation of the Democratic Ligurian Republic to the Kingdom of Sardinia.

It is difficult to estimate the actual impact of all these political upheavals on the people who inhabited the Apennines and on their landscape. It is, however, possible – if not actually probable – that, in the innermost areas, most of the people who lived at the time barely heard of these great changes. For those who walk the Antica Via del Cifalco today, the impression of having entered a world apart, dominated by wild nature and by villages each cradled by its own local traditions, is so powerful that one wonders what the true “History” of this ancient path is, and who its real makers were.
